topological-space.definition:
**拓扑空间**把「邻近」这一概念从距离中解放出来：只保留「哪些集合算开集」这一条信息。设 $X$ 是非空集合，$\tau$ 是幂集 $\mathcal{P}(X)$ 的一个子集族。若 $\tau$ 满足三条**开集公理**，就称 $\tau$ 是 $X$ 上的一个**拓扑**，称 $(X,\tau)$ 是**拓扑空间**，而 $\tau$ 的成员叫 $X$ 的**开集**：
（O1）$\varnothing\in\tau$ 且 $X\in\tau$；
（O2）**任意**多个（有限、可数、甚至不可数无穷多个）$\tau$ 中成员的并仍属于 $\tau$；
（O3）**有限**多个 $\tau$ 中成员的交仍属于 $\tau$。
「任意并、有限交」这一不对称是真正的要点：无限交会出问题。例如 $\mathbb{R}$ 的标准拓扑里每个 $(-\tfrac1n,\tfrac1n)$ 都是开集，可它们的无限交 $\bigcap_{n\ge1}(-\tfrac1n,\tfrac1n)=\{0\}$ 不是开集。只对有限交提要求，开集族既足以充当「邻域」，又足够宽松，使子空间、积、商等构造都能落地。

有了开集就能谈**邻域**：$N\subseteq X$ 称为点 $x$ 的**邻域**，若存在开集 $U$ 使 $x\in U\subseteq N$。请注意**邻域本身不必是开集**：$[0,2]$ 是 $1$ 在 $\mathbb{R}$ 中的邻域，因为它含开集 $(0,2)\ni1$；而 $\{1\}$ 不是 $1$ 的邻域（不含任何含 $1$ 的开集）。$x$ 的一切邻域构成 $x$ 的**邻域系** $\mathcal{N}(x)$，邻域系能反过来重建拓扑：$U$ 开 $\iff$ $U$ 是它每一点的邻域。

最重要的例子来自**度量空间** $(X,d)$：若每个 $x\in U$ 都有开球 $B(x,r)\subseteq U$，就称 $U$ 为开集；这样得到的**度量拓扑**使 $\mathbb{R}$ 上的通常拓扑成为特例（$\mathbb{R}$ 的开集恰是能写成开区间之并的集合）。还有三个必须记住的极端例子：**离散拓扑** $\tau=\mathcal{P}(X)$，每个子集都开，最细；**平凡拓扑**（也叫**密着拓扑**）$\tau=\{\varnothing,X\}$，只有两个开集，最粗；**余有限拓扑** $\tau=\{\varnothing\}\cup\{U\subseteq X: X\setminus U\ \text{是有限集}\}$。同一个集合上可以装彼此不同的拓扑，比较时用「更粗／更细」：$\tau_1\subseteq\tau_2$ 就说 $\tau_1$ 比 $\tau_2$ **粗**。拓扑越细，开集越多、连续映射越少——这条直觉后面处处有用。
topological-space.definitionEn:
A **topological space** frees the idea of being nearby from distance: all that is kept is *which sets count as open*. Let $X$ be a nonempty set and let $\tau$ be a family of subsets of the power set $\mathcal{P}(X)$. If $\tau$ satisfies the three **open-set axioms** it is called a **topology** on $X$, the pair $(X,\tau)$ is a **topological space**, and the members of $\tau$ are the **open sets** of $X$:
(O1) $\varnothing\in\tau$ and $X\in\tau$;
(O2) the union of **arbitrarily many** members of $\tau$ (finitely many, countably many, even uncountably many) still belongs to $\tau$;
(O3) the intersection of **finitely many** members of $\tau$ still belongs to $\tau$.
The asymmetry *arbitrary unions, finite intersections* is the heart of the matter: infinite intersections misbehave. In the usual topology on $\mathbb{R}$ every $(-\tfrac1n,\tfrac1n)$ is open, yet $\bigcap_{n\ge1}(-\tfrac1n,\tfrac1n)=\{0\}$ is not. Demanding only finite intersections keeps the open sets rich enough to serve as neighbourhoods and supple enough for all the standard constructions (subspaces, products, quotients).

Open sets yield **neighbourhoods**: $N\subseteq X$ is a neighbourhood of $x$ if there is an open $U$ with $x\in U\subseteq N$. A neighbourhood need **not** be open: $[0,2]$ is a neighbourhood of $1$ in $\mathbb{R}$ because it contains the open set $(0,2)\ni1$, whereas $\{1\}$ is not. The collection of all neighbourhoods of $x$ is its **neighbourhood system** $\mathcal{N}(x)$, and the topology can be recovered from it: $U$ is open iff it is a neighbourhood of each of its points.

The central example comes from a **metric space** $(X,d)$: call $U$ open if every $x\in U$ admits a ball $B(x,r)\subseteq U$; the resulting **metric topology** makes the usual topology of $\mathbb{R}$ a special case (its open sets are exactly the unions of open intervals). Three extreme examples must be remembered: the **discrete topology** $\tau=\mathcal{P}(X)$, the finest; the **trivial (indiscrete) topology** $\tau=\{\varnothing,X\}$, the coarsest; and the **cofinite topology** $\tau=\{\varnothing\}\cup\{U\subseteq X: X\setminus U\ \text{is finite}\}$. Distinct topologies may live on one set and are compared by inclusion: $\tau_1\subseteq\tau_2$ means $\tau_1$ is **coarser** than $\tau_2$. The finer the topology, the more open sets and the fewer continuous maps — an intuition used throughout.
derivation: 设 $X$ 是非空集合，$\tau\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$。若 (O1) $\varnothing,X\in\tau$；(O2) 对任意指标集 $I$，$U_i\in\tau\ (i\in I)\Rightarrow\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i\in\tau$；(O3) 对任意有限个 $U_1,\dots,U_n\in\tau$，$U_1\cap\cdots\cap U_n\in\tau$，则称 $\tau$ 为 $X$ 上的拓扑，$(X,\tau)$ 为拓扑空间，$\tau$ 的成员为开集。O2 的指标集可以是任意基数，O3 只允许有限交；有限并已含于 O2。反例：$\mathbb R$ 中每个 $(-1/n,1/n)$ 开，但 $\bigcap_{n\ge1}(-1/n,1/n)=\{0\}$ 不开。结论：三条公理的不对称「任意并、有限交」是拓扑定义的核心，不能把 O3 加强为任意交。

由 De Morgan 律，开集的补集给出闭集：称 $F\subseteq X$ 闭，若 $X\setminus F\in\tau$。若 $F_i$ 闭（$i\in I$），则 $X\setminus\bigcap_iF_i=\bigcup_i(X\setminus F_i)$ 开，故任意交闭；若 $F_1,\dots,F_n$ 闭，则 $X\setminus\bigcup_{k=1}^nF_k=\bigcap_{k=1}^n(X\setminus F_k)$ 开，故有限并闭。又 $\varnothing,X$ 既开又闭，称为 clopen。但无限并不必闭：$\bigcup_{n\ge1}[1/n,1]=(0,1]$ 在 $\mathbb R$ 中不闭。结论：闭集族满足「任意交、有限并」，与开集公理对偶；无限并的失败正是 O3 只许有限交的镜像。

邻域：$N\subseteq X$ 是 $x$ 的邻域，若存在开集 $U$ 使 $x\in U\subseteq N$；邻域本身不必开。例如 $[0,2]$ 是 $1$ 在 $\mathbb R$ 中的邻域（含开集 $(0,2)\ni1$），而 $\{1\}$ 不是（不含任何含 $1$ 的开集）。若 $U$ 开，则每个 $x\in U$ 取 $U_x=U$ 即知 $U$ 是其中每点的邻域。反之，若 $U$ 是其中每点的邻域，对每个 $x\in U$ 取开集 $U_x$ 使 $x\in U_x\subseteq U$，则 $U=\bigcup_{x\in U}U_x$，由 O2 开。结论：拓扑可由邻域系完全重建，$U$ 开 $\iff$ $U$ 是其中每点的邻域。

度量拓扑：设 $(X,d)$ 为度量空间，$B(x,r)=\{y\in X:d(x,y)<r\}$。若 $y\in B(x,r)$，令 $\rho=r-d(x,y)>0$；对 $z\in B(y,\rho)$，由三角不等式 $$d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)<d(x,y)+\rho=r,$$ 故 $B(y,\rho)\subseteq B(x,r)$，每个开球开。令 $\tau_d=\{U\subseteq X:\forall x\in U\ \exists r>0,\ B(x,r)\subseteq U\}$；则 $\varnothing,X\in\tau_d$，任意并显然成立，有限交取诸半径的最小值即可。结论：每个度量空间都是拓扑空间，开球全体构成 $\tau_d$ 的基；$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ 语言只是这里的特例。

比较拓扑：若 $\tau_1\subseteq\tau_2$，称 $\tau_1$ 比 $\tau_2$ 粗，$\tau_2$ 比 $\tau_1$ 细。离散拓扑 $\mathcal P(X)$ 最细，平凡拓扑 $\{\varnothing,X\}$ 最粗。恒等映射 $\mathrm{id}:(X,\tau_2)\to(X,\tau_1)$ 连续 $\iff$ 对每个 $U\in\tau_1$，$\mathrm{id}^{-1}(U)=U\in\tau_2$ $\iff$ $\tau_1\subseteq\tau_2$。故定义域越细、目标越粗，连续性越容易。任意多个拓扑的交仍是拓扑：三条公理逐成员验证即可；但并一般不是拓扑，如 $X=\{1,2,3\}$、$\tau_1=\{\varnothing,\{1\},X\}$、$\tau_2=\{\varnothing,\{2\},X\}$ 的并缺少 $\{1,2\}$。结论：拓扑在包含关系下构成完备格，「含给定子族的最粗拓扑」存在，即所有含该子族的拓扑之交。

余有限拓扑：设 $X$ 无限，$\tau_{\mathrm{cof}}=\{\varnothing\}\cup\{U\subseteq X:X\setminus U\ \text{有限}\}$。非空任意并的补是若干有限集之交、仍有限，空并的补为 $X$；有限交的补是有限个有限集之并、仍有限（空交的补为 $\varnothing$），故 $\tau_{\mathrm{cof}}$ 是拓扑。任取非空 $U,V\in\tau_{\mathrm{cof}}$，若 $U\cap V=\varnothing$，则 $X=(X\setminus U)\cup(X\setminus V)$ 有限，矛盾；故任意两个非空开集相交，空间不是 Hausdorff 的。度量空间中 $x\ne y$ 时 $B(x,d(x,y)/2)$ 与 $B(y,d(x,y)/2)$ 不交，故度量空间必 Hausdorff。结论：无限集上的余有限拓扑不可度量化；拓扑空间确实严格广于度量空间，分离性正是衡量差距的工具。
derivationEn: Let $X$ be a nonempty set and $\tau\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$. Then $\tau$ is a topology on $X$, and $(X,\tau)$ a topological space, if (O1) $\varnothing,X\in\tau$; (O2) for every index set $I$, $U_i\in\tau$ for all $i\in I$ implies $\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i\in\tau$; (O3) for any finitely many $U_1,\dots,U_n\in\tau$, $U_1\cap\cdots\cap U_n\in\tau$. The members of $\tau$ are the open sets. The index set in O2 may have arbitrary cardinality, while O3 allows only finite intersections; finite unions are already included in O2. Counterexample: in $\mathbb R$ each $(-1/n,1/n)$ is open, but $\bigcap_{n\ge1}(-1/n,1/n)=\{0\}$ is not. Conclusion: the asymmetry "arbitrary unions, finite intersections" is the heart of the definition, and O3 cannot be strengthened to arbitrary intersections.

By De Morgan's laws the complements of open sets give the closed sets: $F\subseteq X$ is closed if $X\setminus F\in\tau$. If $F_i$ is closed for $i\in I$, then $X\setminus\bigcap_iF_i=\bigcup_i(X\setminus F_i)$ is open, so arbitrary intersections of closed sets are closed; if $F_1,\dots,F_n$ are closed, then $X\setminus\bigcup_{k=1}^nF_k=\bigcap_{k=1}^n(X\setminus F_k)$ is open, so finite unions are closed. Also $\varnothing$ and $X$ are both open and closed (clopen). Infinite unions need not be closed: $\bigcup_{n\ge1}[1/n,1]=(0,1]$ is not closed in $\mathbb R$. Conclusion: closed sets satisfy "arbitrary intersections, finite unions", dual to the open-set axioms; the failure for infinite unions mirrors the restriction to finite intersections.

Neighborhoods: $N\subseteq X$ is a neighborhood of $x$ if there is an open $U$ with $x\in U\subseteq N$; $N$ itself need not be open. For example $[0,2]$ is a neighborhood of $1$ in $\mathbb R$ (it contains the open set $(0,2)\ni1$), while $\{1\}$ is not (it contains no open set containing $1$). If $U$ is open, then for each $x\in U$ taking $U_x=U$ shows that $U$ is a neighborhood of each of its points. Conversely, if $U$ is a neighborhood of each of its points, choose for each $x\in U$ an open $U_x$ with $x\in U_x\subseteq U$; then $U=\bigcup_{x\in U}U_x$ is open by O2. Conclusion: the topology is completely recovered from the neighborhood systems, and $U$ is open iff it is a neighborhood of each of its points.

Metric topology: let $(X,d)$ be a metric space and $B(x,r)=\{y\in X:d(x,y)<r\}$. If $y\in B(x,r)$, put $\rho=r-d(x,y)>0$; for $z\in B(y,\rho)$ the triangle inequality gives $$d(x,z)\le d(x,y)+d(y,z)<d(x,y)+\rho=r,$$ so $B(y,\rho)\subseteq B(x,r)$ and every ball is open. Let $\tau_d=\{U\subseteq X:\forall x\in U\ \exists r>0,\ B(x,r)\subseteq U\}$. Then $\varnothing,X\in\tau_d$, arbitrary unions are immediate, and for finite intersections one takes the minimum of the finitely many radii. Conclusion: every metric space is a topological space and the open balls form a basis for $\tau_d$; the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ language is the special case of this construction.

Comparing topologies: if $\tau_1\subseteq\tau_2$, then $\tau_1$ is coarser and $\tau_2$ finer. The discrete topology $\mathcal P(X)$ is the finest and the trivial topology $\{\varnothing,X\}$ the coarsest. The identity $\mathrm{id}:(X,\tau_2)\to(X,\tau_1)$ is continuous iff for every $U\in\tau_1$, $\mathrm{id}^{-1}(U)=U\in\tau_2$, i.e. iff $\tau_1\subseteq\tau_2$. Hence a finer domain and a coarser target make continuity easier. An arbitrary intersection of topologies is again a topology (check the three axioms member by member), but a union need not be: for $X=\{1,2,3\}$, $\tau_1=\{\varnothing,\{1\},X\}$ and $\tau_2=\{\varnothing,\{2\},X\}$ have a union lacking $\{1,2\}$. Conclusion: topologies form a complete lattice under inclusion, and the coarsest topology containing a given family exists as the intersection of all topologies containing it.

Cofinite topology: let $X$ be infinite and $\tau_{\mathrm{cof}}=\{\varnothing\}\cup\{U\subseteq X:X\setminus U\ \text{is finite}\}$. The complement of a nonempty arbitrary union is an intersection of finite sets, hence finite, and the empty union has complement $X$; the complement of a finite intersection is a finite union of finite sets, hence finite (the empty intersection has complement $\varnothing$); so $\tau_{\mathrm{cof}}$ is a topology. If $U,V\in\tau_{\mathrm{cof}}$ are nonempty and $U\cap V=\varnothing$, then $X=(X\setminus U)\cup(X\setminus V)$ is finite, a contradiction; hence any two nonempty open sets meet and the space is not Hausdorff. In a metric space, for $x\ne y$ the balls $B(x,d(x,y)/2)$ and $B(y,d(x,y)/2)$ are disjoint, so every metric space is Hausdorff. Conclusion: the cofinite topology on an infinite set is not metrizable; topological spaces are strictly more general than metric spaces, and separation axioms measure the gap.

formulas.note: 公理 O1：空集与全集都是开集（于是它们也既开又闭）。
formulas.noteEn: Axiom O1: the empty set and the whole space are open (hence also closed).

formulas.note: 公理 O2：**任意**多个开集的并是开集；指标集 $I$ 可以是任意大的无限集。
formulas.noteEn: Axiom O2: the union of **arbitrarily many** open sets is open; the index set $I$ may be infinite of any size.

formulas.note: 公理 O3：**有限**多个开集的交是开集；无限交一般不成立（$\bigcap_{n}(-\frac1n,\frac1n)=\{0\}$）。
formulas.noteEn: Axiom O3: the intersection of **finitely many** open sets is open; infinite intersections generally fail ($\bigcap_n(-\frac1n,\frac1n)=\{0\}$).

formulas.latex: N\ \text{是}\ x\ \text{的邻域}\iff \exists\,U\in\tau:\ x\in U\subseteq N
formulas.note: 邻域的定义：只要含一个含 $x$ 的开集即可，邻域自身不必是开集。
formulas.noteEn: Definition of a neighbourhood: it suffices to contain an open set containing $x$; the neighbourhood itself need not be open.

formulas.note: 度量拓扑的定义；此时全体开球 $B(x,r)$ 成为该拓扑的一组基。
formulas.noteEn: The metric topology: a set is open when every point has a ball inside it; the balls form a basis for this topology.

properties: 开集族对任意并、有限交封闭；对偶地，闭集族对任意交、有限并封闭（两者方向正好互换）
由邻域系可完全重建拓扑：$U$ 开 $\iff$ $U$ 是其中每一点的邻域
拓扑可按粗细比较：$\tau_1\subseteq\tau_2$ 时 $\tau_1$ 粗、$\tau_2$ 细；$X$ 上全体拓扑在包含关系下构成完备格（任意多个拓扑之交仍是拓扑，并一般不是）
「含给定子族的最粗拓扑」总存在（取含该子族的一切拓扑之交），子空间与积拓扑由此而来；商拓扑是对偶的另一极——使商映射连续的**最细**拓扑
并非每个拓扑都来自度量：无限集上的余有限拓扑中任意两个非空开集都相交，不是 Hausdorff 的，因而不可度量化
propertiesEn: Open sets are closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections; dually, closed sets are closed under arbitrary intersections and finite unions (the two directions are interchanged)
The topology is fully determined by the neighbourhood systems: $U$ is open iff $U$ is a neighbourhood of each of its points

Topologies are compared by inclusion: $\tau_1\subseteq\tau_2$ makes $\tau_1$ coarser and $\tau_2$ finer; the topologies on $X$ form a complete lattice under inclusion (arbitrary intersections are topologies, unions in general are not)

The coarsest topology containing a given family always exists (intersect all topologies containing it); subspaces and products arise this way; the quotient topology is the opposite extreme — the **finest** topology making the quotient map continuous
Not every topology comes from a metric: in the cofinite topology on an infinite set any two nonempty open sets meet, so it is not Hausdorff and hence not metrisable

examples.problem: 设 $X$ 是无限集，$\tau=\{\varnothing\}\cup\{U\subseteq X: X\setminus U\ \text{有限}\}$ 是余有限拓扑。验证 $\tau$ 满足三条开集公理，并说明它不满足 Hausdorff 性质。
examples.solution:
（O1）$\varnothing\in\tau$；又 $X\setminus X=\varnothing$ 有限，故 $X\in\tau$。
（O2）设 $U_i\in\tau$（$i\in I$）。若所有 $U_i$ 都空，则并也空，属于 $\tau$；否则取某个非空 $U_{i_0}$，于是 $X\setminus\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i\subseteq X\setminus U_{i_0}$ 有限，故 $\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i\in\tau$。
（O3）设 $U_1,\dots,U_n\in\tau$。若某个 $U_j=\varnothing$，交即 $\varnothing\in\tau$；否则 $X\setminus\bigcap_{k=1}^{n}U_k=\bigcup_{k=1}^{n}(X\setminus U_k)$ 是有限多个有限集之并，仍有限，故 $\bigcap_{k=1}^{n}U_k\in\tau$。
最后取任意两个非空开集 $U,V$：$X\setminus(U\cap V)=(X\setminus U)\cup(X\setminus V)$ 是有限集，而 $X$ 无限，故 $U\cap V\ne\varnothing$。任意两个非空开集都相交，无法用不相交开集分离两点，所以不是 Hausdorff 空间。

examples.problem: 在 $\mathbb{R}$ 的标准拓扑中，举出无限多个开集使其交不是开集；再写出对偶的闭集例子。
examples.solution:
取 $U_n=(-\tfrac1n,\tfrac1n)$（$n\ge1$），每个 $U_n$ 都是开集，但 $\bigcap_{n\ge1}U_n=\{0\}$ 不是开集：$0$ 的任何邻域都含非零点。同理 $\bigcap_{n\ge1}(-\tfrac1n,1+\tfrac1n)=[0,1]$ 也不是开集。这说明公理 O3 里的「有限」不能改成「无限」。
对偶地取闭集 $F_n=[\tfrac1n,1]$，每个 $F_n$ 都闭，而 $\bigcup_{n\ge1}F_n=(0,1]$ 不是闭集：$0$ 是它的聚点但不属于它。

expression.text: (X, τ)：集合 X 配上一族满足 O1–O3 的开集 τ；开集就是 τ 的成员
expression.note: 拓扑只记得「哪些集合开」，不记得距离；同一集合上可以有粗细不同的多个拓扑。
expression.noteEn: A topology records only which sets are open, not distances; one set may carry many topologies of different coarseness.

basis-subbasis.definition:
**基**让我们用较少的集合生成全部开集。设 $(X,\tau)$ 是拓扑空间，$\mathcal{B}\subseteq\tau$。若每个开集都能写成 $\mathcal{B}$ 中若干成员的并（空并约定为 $\varnothing$），就称 $\mathcal{B}$ 是 $\tau$ 的**基**（拓扑基）。实际检验时用点式说法更方便：$U$ 是开集 $\iff$ 对每个 $x\in U$ 存在 $B\in\mathcal{B}$ 使 $x\in B\subseteq U$。由 $\mathcal{B}$ 生成的拓扑是 $\tau(\mathcal{B})=\{\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal{B}'}B: \mathcal{B}'\subseteq\mathcal{B}\}$，它是**含 $\mathcal{B}$ 的最粗（最小）拓扑**，也就是一切含 $\mathcal{B}$ 的拓扑之交。

**判定定理（两条都要）**：子族 $\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(X)$ 是 $X$ 上某个拓扑的基，当且仅当
（B1）$\mathcal{B}$ 覆盖 $X$，即 $\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal{B}}B=X$；
（B2）若 $B_1,B_2\in\mathcal{B}$ 且 $x\in B_1\cap B_2$，则存在 $B_3\in\mathcal{B}$ 使 $x\in B_3\subseteq B_1\cap B_2$。
B1 保证 $X$ 本身是基元之并（缺少它，生成的集族里没有 $X$，不是拓扑）；B2 保证两个基元之交也是基元之并，从而是开集（缺少它，交就可能不再开集）。等价地，在 B1 成立时，B2 可以叙述成一句漂亮的话：**任意两个基元之交是若干基元之并**。

**子基**再往前走一步。若 $\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(X)$ 的所有**有限交**构成一个基，就称 $\mathcal{S}$ 是拓扑的**子基**。约定 $0$ 个集合的交为 $X$，于是有限交族 $\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{S}}$ 自动覆盖 $X$——条件 B1 自动成立；而 B2 也自动成立（两个有限交之交仍是有限交）。因此**任意子族 $\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(X)$ 都是某个拓扑的子基**，这个拓扑就是含 $\mathcal{S}$ 的最粗拓扑，它的开集恰好是若干有限交之并。这让子基成为最省力的定义工具：想造一个拓扑，只需指定几个集合作子基，然后取它能生成的最粗拓扑。

例子：$\mathbb{R}$ 的标准拓扑可由子基 $\{(-\infty,a): a\in\mathbb{R}\}\cup\{(b,+\infty): b\in\mathbb{R}\}$ 生成，因为当 $b<a$ 时两个成员的有限交 $(-\infty,a)\cap(b,+\infty)=(b,a)$ 正是有界开区间（$b\ge a$ 时交为 $\varnothing$，也无妨）。积拓扑取 $\{\pi_i^{-1}(U_i)\}$ 为子基，弱拓扑、Zariski 拓扑也都是这样定义的。还要记住基不唯一：$\mathbb{R}$ 上全体开区间、全体有理端点开区间、全体有理心有理半径的开球都生成同一个标准拓扑——这正是第二可数性的雏形。
basis-subbasis.definitionEn:
A **basis** generates all open sets from a smaller family. Let $(X,\tau)$ be a topological space and $\mathcal{B}\subseteq\tau$. It is a **basis** for $\tau$ if every open set is a union of members of $\mathcal{B}$ (the empty union being $\varnothing$). The practical pointwise test is: $U$ is open iff every $x\in U$ lies in some $B\in\mathcal{B}$ with $B\subseteq U$. The topology generated by $\mathcal{B}$ is $\tau(\mathcal{B})=\{\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal{B}'}B:\ \mathcal{B}'\subseteq\mathcal{B}\}$, the **coarsest (smallest) topology containing $\mathcal{B}$**, i.e. the intersection of all topologies containing it.

**Criterion (both conditions are required).** A family $\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(X)$ is a basis for some topology on $X$ iff
(B1) $\mathcal{B}$ covers $X$: $\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal{B}}B=X$;
(B2) whenever $B_1,B_2\in\mathcal{B}$ and $x\in B_1\cap B_2$, there is $B_3\in\mathcal{B}$ with $x\in B_3\subseteq B_1\cap B_2$.
(B1) makes $X$ itself a union of basis elements — without it the generated family lacks $X$ and is no topology; (B2) makes the intersection of two basis elements a union of basis elements, hence open. Equivalently, given (B1), condition (B2) says: the intersection of any two basis elements is a union of basis elements.

A **subbasis** goes one step further. If the **finite intersections** of a family $\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(X)$ form a basis, $\mathcal{S}$ is called a **subbasis**. By convention the empty intersection is $X$, so the family $\mathcal{B}_{\mathcal{S}}$ of finite intersections automatically covers $X$ (condition (B1) is free) and satisfies (B2) (the intersection of two finite intersections is again a finite intersection). Hence **every** family $\mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(X)$ is a subbasis for some topology — the coarsest topology containing $\mathcal{S}$, whose open sets are exactly the unions of finite intersections of members of $\mathcal{S}$. This makes subbases the cheapest way to define a topology: specify a few sets and take the coarsest topology containing them.

Examples: the usual topology of $\mathbb{R}$ is generated by the subbasis $\{(-\infty,a):a\in\mathbb{R}\}\cup\{(b,+\infty):b\in\mathbb{R}\}$, since for $b<a$ the intersection of one member of each part equals the bounded open interval $(b,a)$ (and for $b\ge a$ it is empty, which is harmless). The product topology uses the sets $\pi_i^{-1}(U_i)$ as a subbasis, and weak and Zariski topologies are defined the same way. Bases are far from unique: all open intervals, all open intervals with rational endpoints, and all balls with rational centre and radius generate the same topology on $\mathbb{R}$ — the germ of second countability.
derivation: 设 $(X,\tau)$ 为拓扑空间，$\mathcal B\subseteq\tau$。若每个 $U\in\tau$ 都可写成 $\mathcal B$ 中若干成员的并（空并为 $\varnothing$），称 $\mathcal B$ 为 $\tau$ 的基。点式判别：$U$ 开 $\iff$ 对每个 $x\in U$ 存在 $B\in\mathcal B$ 使 $x\in B\subseteq U$。证明：若 $\mathcal B$ 是基且 $x\in U=\bigcup_\alpha B_\alpha$，则 $x$ 属于某个 $B_\alpha\subseteq U$；反之若点式条件成立，则 $U=\bigcup_{x\in U}B_x$，其中 $B_x\subseteq U$，故 $U$ 是基元之并。结论：基把「验证整个开集」化为「逐点找基元夹住」，这是后面判定定理的出发点。

生成：对任意 $\mathcal B\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$，令 $\tau(\mathcal B)=\{\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal B'}B:\mathcal B'\subseteq\mathcal B\}$。它对任意并封闭（并的并仍是并），含 $\varnothing$（空并），且任何含 $\mathcal B$ 的拓扑必含所有基元之并，故只要 $\tau(\mathcal B)$ 是拓扑，它就是含 $\mathcal B$ 的最粗拓扑。但 $\tau(\mathcal B)$ 未必对有限交封闭；例如 $X=\{1,2,3\}$、$\mathcal B=\{\{1,2\},\{2,3\}\}$ 时 $\{1,2\}\cap\{2,3\}=\{2\}$ 不是基元之并。若 $\mathcal B$ 不覆盖 $X$，则 $\tau(\mathcal B)$ 连 $X$ 都不含（如 $X=\{1,2\}$、$\mathcal B=\{\{1\}\}$）。结论：要让「基元之并」成为拓扑，必须另外验证两条附加条件。

判定定理：$\mathcal B\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ 是某个拓扑的基 $\iff$ (B1) $\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal B}B=X$；(B2) 若 $B_1,B_2\in\mathcal B$、$x\in B_1\cap B_2$，则存在 $B_3\in\mathcal B$ 使 $x\in B_3\subseteq B_1\cap B_2$。必要性：$X$ 开故被覆盖；$B_1\cap B_2$ 开，故其中每点有基元夹在中间。充分性：令 $\tau$ 为所有基元之并；B1 给 $X$，空并给 $\varnothing$，任意并显然；只需验证二元交：若 $U=\bigcup_\alpha B_\alpha$、$V=\bigcup_\beta C_\beta$，对 $x\in U\cap V$ 取 $B_\alpha,C_\beta\ni x$，由 B2 取 $D_x$ 使 $x\in D_x\subseteq B_\alpha\cap C_\beta\subseteq U\cap V$，于是 $U\cap V=\bigcup_{x\in U\cap V}D_x$ 开。结论：B1、B2 是基的充要条件；B1 是覆盖条件，B2 是逐点局部条件。

两条条件独立：$X=\{1,2,3\}$、$\mathcal B=\{\{1,2\},\{2,3\}\}$ 满足 B1，但 $2\in\{1,2\}\cap\{2,3\}=\{2\}$ 而不存在基元含于 $\{2\}$，故 B2 失败；$X=\{1,2\}$、$\mathcal B=\{\{1\}\}$ 的 B2 成立（取 $B_3=\{1\}$），但不覆盖 $2$，故 B1 失败。度量空间中开球族满足 B1（$X=\bigcup_{x}B(x,1)$）与 B2：若 $x\in B(x_1,r_1)\cap B(x_2,r_2)$，取 $$r=\min\{r_1-d(x,x_1),\ r_2-d(x,x_2)\}>0,$$ 则对 $y\in B(x,r)$ 有 $d(y,x_i)\le d(y,x)+d(x,x_i)<r_i$，故 $B(x,r)\subseteq B(x_1,r_1)\cap B(x_2,r_2)$。结论：两条条件各管一件事，缺一不可；度量球是 B1+B2 的标准范例。

子基：设 $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$，令 $$\mathcal B_{\mathcal S}=\Bigl\{\bigcap_{k=1}^n S_k:\ n\ge0,\ S_k\in\mathcal S\Bigr\},$$ 约定 $n=0$ 时交为 $X$。则 $\mathcal B_{\mathcal S}$ 自动满足 B1（$X$ 是空交）与 B2（两个有限交之交仍是有限交，取 $B_3=B_1\cap B_2$），故它是某个拓扑的基；称 $\mathcal S$ 为该拓扑的子基，生成的拓扑是 $\mathcal S$ 的有限交之任意并，即含 $\mathcal S$ 的最粗拓扑。特别地，任意 $\mathcal S$ 都是某个拓扑的子基，无需额外条件。结论：子基是最省力的拓扑生成工具：先取有限交得基，再取任意并得拓扑。

例：$\mathbb R$ 的标准拓扑由子基 $\mathcal S=\{(-\infty,a):a\in\mathbb R\}\cup\{(b,+\infty):b\in\mathbb R\}$ 生成；两个成员的有限交为 $(b,a)$（$b<a$）、射线、$\varnothing$ 或 $\mathbb R$，再取任意并即得全部开集。积拓扑也以 $\{\pi_i^{-1}(U_i):U_i\ \text{开}\}$ 为子基。连续性的子基判据：$f:X\to Y$ 连续 $\iff$ 对目标空间某个子基的每个成员 $S$，$f^{-1}(S)$ 开。证明：任一开集 $V=\bigcup_\alpha\bigcap_{k=1}^{n_\alpha}S_{\alpha,k}$，于是 $$f^{-1}(V)=\bigcup_\alpha\bigcap_{k=1}^{n_\alpha}f^{-1}(S_{\alpha,k})$$ 是开集之并。结论：验证连续性只需查一组生成元，基或子基均可，这正是不必逐个开集验证的原因。
derivationEn: Let $(X,\tau)$ be a topological space and $\mathcal B\subseteq\tau$. If every $U\in\tau$ is a union of members of $\mathcal B$ (the empty union being $\varnothing$), then $\mathcal B$ is a basis for $\tau$. Pointwise test: $U$ is open iff for every $x\in U$ there is $B\in\mathcal B$ with $x\in B\subseteq U$. Proof: if $\mathcal B$ is a basis and $x\in U=\bigcup_\alpha B_\alpha$, then $x$ lies in some $B_\alpha\subseteq U$; conversely, if the pointwise condition holds, then $U=\bigcup_{x\in U}B_x$ with $B_x\subseteq U$, so $U$ is a union of basis elements. Conclusion: a basis replaces the verification of a whole open set by a pointwise search for a basis element squeezed inside it, which is the starting point of the criterion below.

Generation: for any $\mathcal B\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ put $\tau(\mathcal B)=\{\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal B'}B:\mathcal B'\subseteq\mathcal B\}$. It is closed under arbitrary unions (a union of unions is a union), contains $\varnothing$ (empty union), and every topology containing $\mathcal B$ must contain all unions of members of $\mathcal B$; hence, provided $\tau(\mathcal B)$ is a topology, it is the coarsest topology containing $\mathcal B$. But $\tau(\mathcal B)$ need not be closed under finite intersections: for $X=\{1,2,3\}$ and $\mathcal B=\{\{1,2\},\{2,3\}\}$, the set $\{1,2\}\cap\{2,3\}=\{2\}$ is not a union of basis elements. If $\mathcal B$ does not cover $X$, then $\tau(\mathcal B)$ does not even contain $X$ (e.g. $X=\{1,2\}$, $\mathcal B=\{\{1\}\}$). Conclusion: for the unions of a family to form a topology, two additional conditions must be imposed.

Basis criterion: $\mathcal B\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ is a basis for some topology iff (B1) $\bigcup_{B\in\mathcal B}B=X$; (B2) whenever $B_1,B_2\in\mathcal B$ and $x\in B_1\cap B_2$, there is $B_3\in\mathcal B$ with $x\in B_3\subseteq B_1\cap B_2$. Necessity: $X$ is open, so it is covered; $B_1\cap B_2$ is open, so through each of its points passes a basis element contained in it. Sufficiency: let $\tau$ be the family of all unions of basis elements; B1 gives $X$, the empty union gives $\varnothing$, arbitrary unions are clear, and only binary intersections need checking. If $U=\bigcup_\alpha B_\alpha$ and $V=\bigcup_\beta C_\beta$, then for $x\in U\cap V$ choose $B_\alpha,C_\beta\ni x$ and use B2 to find $D_x$ with $x\in D_x\subseteq B_\alpha\cap C_\beta\subseteq U\cap V$; hence $U\cap V=\bigcup_{x\in U\cap V}D_x$ is open. Conclusion: B1 and B2 are necessary and sufficient; B1 is a covering condition and B2 a pointwise local one.

The two conditions are independent: on $X=\{1,2,3\}$, $\mathcal B=\{\{1,2\},\{2,3\}\}$ satisfies B1, but $2\in\{1,2\}\cap\{2,3\}=\{2\}$ and no basis element is contained in $\{2\}$, so B2 fails; on $X=\{1,2\}$, $\mathcal B=\{\{1\}\}$ satisfies B2 (take $B_3=\{1\}$) but does not cover $2$, so B1 fails. In a metric space the balls satisfy B1 ($X=\bigcup_xB(x,1)$) and B2: if $x\in B(x_1,r_1)\cap B(x_2,r_2)$, take $$r=\min\{r_1-d(x,x_1),\ r_2-d(x,x_2)\}>0;$$ then for $y\in B(x,r)$, $d(y,x_i)\le d(y,x)+d(x,x_i)<r_i$, so $B(x,r)\subseteq B(x_1,r_1)\cap B(x_2,r_2)$. Conclusion: each condition governs a different point, and neither can be dropped; metric balls are the standard example satisfying both.

Subbasis: for $\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ put $$\mathcal B_{\mathcal S}=\Bigl\{\bigcap_{k=1}^n S_k:\ n\ge0,\ S_k\in\mathcal S\Bigr\},$$ with the empty intersection ($n=0$) defined to be $X$. Then $\mathcal B_{\mathcal S}$ automatically satisfies B1 ($X$ is the empty intersection) and B2 (the intersection of two finite intersections is again a finite intersection; take $B_3=B_1\cap B_2$), so it is a basis for a topology. One calls $\mathcal S$ a subbasis for that topology; the topology is the family of arbitrary unions of finite intersections of members of $\mathcal S$, i.e. the coarsest topology containing $\mathcal S$. In particular every $\mathcal S$ is a subbasis for some topology, with no extra condition. Conclusion: a subbasis is the most economical generator: first take finite intersections to get a basis, then arbitrary unions to get the topology.

Example: the standard topology of $\mathbb R$ is generated by the subbasis $\mathcal S=\{(-\infty,a):a\in\mathbb R\}\cup\{(b,+\infty):b\in\mathbb R\}$; the finite intersections of two members are $(b,a)$ when $b<a$, rays, $\varnothing$, or $\mathbb R$, and arbitrary unions then give all open sets. The product topology is likewise generated by the subbasis $\{\pi_i^{-1}(U_i):U_i\ \text{open}\}$. Subbasis test for continuity: $f:X\to Y$ is continuous iff $f^{-1}(S)$ is open for every member $S$ of some subbasis of $Y$. Indeed, every open $V$ is $\bigcup_\alpha\bigcap_{k=1}^{n_\alpha}S_{\alpha,k}$, so $$f^{-1}(V)=\bigcup_\alpha\bigcap_{k=1}^{n_\alpha}f^{-1}(S_{\alpha,k})$$ is a union of open sets. Conclusion: continuity need only be checked on a generating family, a basis or a subbasis, which is why one never checks every open set individually.

formulas.latex: U\in\tau\iff \forall x\in U\ \exists\,B\in\mathcal{B}:\ x\in B\subseteq U
formulas.note: 基的点式判别法：只要每点的某邻域能「夹」在基元与开集之间即可。
formulas.noteEn: The pointwise test for a basis: near each point some basis element must be squeezed between the point and the open set.

formulas.note: 由基生成的拓扑：所有基元之并的全体；空并给出 $\varnothing$。
formulas.noteEn: The topology generated by a basis: all unions of basis elements, the empty union giving $\varnothing$.

formulas.note: 第一条判定条件：基必须覆盖整个空间，否则生成的集族里没有 $X$。
formulas.noteEn: First criterion: the basis must cover the whole space, otherwise $X$ itself is missing from the generated family.

formulas.latex: (B2)\quad x\in B_1\cap B_2,\ B_1,B_2\in\mathcal{B}\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists\,B_3\in\mathcal{B}:\ x\in B_3\subseteq B_1\cap B_2
formulas.note: 第二条判定条件：两个基元之交中每点都含在一个含于该交的基元里（等价说法：两基元之交是若干基元之并）。
formulas.noteEn: Second criterion: through each point of an intersection of two basis elements passes a basis element contained in that intersection (equivalently, the intersection is a union of basis elements).

formulas.note: 子基的有限交族是基（$n=0$ 时约定交为 $X$）；它生成的就是含 $\mathcal{S}$ 的**最粗**拓扑。
formulas.noteEn: The finite intersections of a subbasis form a basis (the empty intersection is $X$), and they generate the **coarsest** topology containing $\mathcal{S}$.

properties: B2 的等价形式：任意两个基元之交可写成若干基元之并（在 B1 成立的前提下）
度量空间中开球全体是度量拓扑的基；验证 B2 时只需取 $r=\min\{r_1-d(x,x_1),\ r_2-d(x,x_2)\}>0$，则 $B(x,r)\subseteq B(x_1,r_1)\cap B(x_2,r_2)$
同一拓扑可以有成员不同而粗细相同的多种基；有可数基的拓扑称为第二可数，$\mathbb{R}$ 的标准拓扑由「有理端点开区间」给出可数基
任意子族都是某拓扑的子基，它生成的是含该子族的最粗拓扑；判断映射连续时也只需对目标空间某个子基的成员验证原像是开集
propertiesEn: Both criteria matter: $\{\{1,2\},\{2,3\}\}$ satisfies (B1) but not (B2), while $\{\{1\}\}$ on $X=\{1,2\}$ satisfies (B2) but not (B1)
Equivalent form of (B2), given (B1): the intersection of any two basis elements is a union of basis elements
In a metric space the balls form a basis; to check (B2) take $r=\min\{r_1-d(x,x_1),\ r_2-d(x,x_2)\}>0$, so that $B(x,r)\subseteq B(x_1,r_1)\cap B(x_2,r_2)$
One topology has many different bases of the same coarseness; a topology with a countable basis is called second countable, and rational-ended open intervals give one for $\mathbb{R}$
Every family is a subbasis for some topology, namely the coarsest one containing it; continuity of a map need only be checked on the preimages of the members of a subbasis of the target

examples.problem: 设 $X=\mathbb{R}$，$\mathcal{S}=\{(-\infty,a): a\in\mathbb{R}\}\cup\{(b,+\infty): b\in\mathbb{R}\}$。证明 $\mathcal{S}$ 生成的拓扑恰是 $\mathbb{R}$ 上的标准拓扑。
examples.solution:
记 $\tau_{\mathcal{S}}$ 为由 $\mathcal{S}$ 生成的拓扑（含 $\mathcal{S}$ 的最粗拓扑），$\tau_{\mathrm{std}}$ 为标准拓扑。
（1）$\tau_{\mathcal{S}}\subseteq\tau_{\mathrm{std}}$：每个 $(-\infty,a)$ 与 $(b,+\infty)$ 都是标准开集，故 $\tau_{\mathrm{std}}$ 是含 $\mathcal{S}$ 的拓扑；而 $\tau_{\mathcal{S}}$ 是这类拓扑中最粗的，故它最小。
（2）$\tau_{\mathrm{std}}\subseteq\tau_{\mathcal{S}}$：任取 $U\in\tau_{\mathrm{std}}$ 与 $x\in U$，由标准拓扑的定义存在 $\varepsilon>0$ 使 $(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)\subseteq U$。而
$(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)=(-\infty,x+\varepsilon)\cap(x-\varepsilon,+\infty)$
是两个子基成员的有限交，含 $x$ 且含于 $U$。于是 $U$ 是若干这样的有限交之并，属于 $\tau_{\mathcal{S}}$。
两向包含合并得 $\tau_{\mathcal{S}}=\tau_{\mathrm{std}}$，即标准拓扑恰是能使所有射线都开的最粗拓扑。

（a）B1 成立：$\{1,2\}\cup\{2,3\}=X$。但 B2 失败：$2\in\{1,2\}\cap\{2,3\}=\{2\}$，而 $\mathcal{B}$ 中含 $2$ 的成员只有 $\{1,2\}$ 与 $\{2,3\}$，都不含于 $\{2\}$，故找不到所需的 $B_3$。若 $\mathcal{B}$ 真是某拓扑的基，则该拓扑中 $\{1,2\}\cap\{2,3\}=\{2\}$ 必须是开集，但 $\{2\}$ 无法写成基元之并，矛盾。
（b）只有一个成员，B2 自动成立（$\{1\}\cap\{1\}=\{1\}\supseteq\{1\}$）；但 B1 失败：$\{1\}\ne X$。由它生成的集族是 $\{\varnothing,\{1\}\}$，其中没有 $X=\{1,2\}$，不是拓扑。可见两条条件各有不可替代的作用。

closed-sets-interior.definition:
$A\subseteq X$ 称为**闭集**，若它的补集 $X\setminus A$ 是开集。**方向务必记准：闭 = 补开**。由此立刻得到与开集公理对偶的三条**闭集公理**：（C1）$\varnothing$ 与 $X$ 都是闭集；（C2）**任意**多个闭集的交是闭集；（C3）**有限**多个闭集的并是闭集。请对比开集公理——开集是「任意并、有限交」，闭集是「任意交、有限并」，两个方向正好互换。「闭」不等于「非开」：$\mathbb{R}$ 中 $[0,1)$ 既不开也不闭，而 $\varnothing$ 与 $\mathbb{R}$ 既开又闭（简称 clopen）。无限多个闭集的并可以不是闭集：$\bigcup_{n\ge1}[\tfrac1n,1]=(0,1]$。

含 $A$ 的最小闭集 $\overline{A}=\bigcap\{F\subseteq X: F\ \text{闭},\ A\subseteq F\}$ 称为 $A$ 的**闭包**。它有两套常用的等价刻画：其一，$x\in\overline{A}$ $\iff$ $x$ 的每个邻域与 $A$ 相交（只需每个开邻域与 $A$ 相交）；其二，$\overline{A}=A\cup A'$，其中 $A'$ 是 $A$ 的**导集**——$x\in A'$ 时称 $x$ 为 $A$ 的**聚点**（极限点），意思是 $x$ 的**每个**邻域都与 $A\setminus\{x\}$ 相交。聚点不必属于 $A$：$0$ 是 $(0,1)$ 的聚点；$A$ 中的点也未必是聚点：若存在邻域 $N$ 使 $N\cap A=\{x\}$，则称 $x$ 是 $A$ 的**孤立点**（如 $\mathbb{Z}\subset\mathbb{R}$ 的每个点）。于是有干净的等价链：$A$ 闭 $\iff A'\subseteq A\iff A=\overline{A}$。

对偶地，$\operatorname{int}A=\bigcup\{U\in\tau: U\subseteq A\}=X\setminus\overline{X\setminus A}$ 称为 $A$ 的**内部**，即含于 $A$ 的最大开集，其成员叫**内点**（有邻域完全落在 $A$ 中）。$\partial A=\overline{A}\cap\overline{X\setminus A}$ 称为 $A$ 的**边界**，它把整个空间切成互不相交的三块：$X=\operatorname{int}A\ \sqcup\ \partial A\ \sqcup\ \operatorname{int}(X\setminus A)$。若 $\overline{A}=X$，称 $A$ **稠密**于 $X$（等价于 $A$ 与每个非空开集相交），例如 $\mathbb{Q}$ 在 $\mathbb{R}$ 中稠密；若 $\operatorname{int}\overline{A}=\varnothing$，称 $A$ **无处稠密**（$\mathbb{Z}$ 在 $\mathbb{R}$ 中无处稠密且没有聚点；而 Cantor 集同样无处稠密，却点点都是聚点——可见「无处稠密」与「没有聚点」是两回事）。可数多个无处稠密集之并叫**第一纲**集，不是第一纲的叫**第二纲**集。**Baire 纲定理**断言：完备度量空间（更一般地，局部紧 Hausdorff 空间）是第二纲的——「不能写成可数个无处稠密集之并」这一条，是许多存在性定理的支点。
closed-sets-interior.definitionEn:
A set $A\subseteq X$ is **closed** if its complement $X\setminus A$ is open. **Remember the direction: closed means the complement is open.** This immediately gives the three **closed-set axioms**, dual to the open-set axioms: (C1) $\varnothing$ and $X$ are closed; (C2) the intersection of **arbitrarily many** closed sets is closed; (C3) the union of **finitely many** closed sets is closed. Compare the open-set axioms — open sets allow arbitrary unions and finite intersections, closed sets allow arbitrary intersections and finite unions, the two directions being interchanged. Closed does not mean not open: in $\mathbb{R}$ the set $[0,1)$ is neither open nor closed, while $\varnothing$ and $\mathbb{R}$ are both (they are called clopen). An infinite union of closed sets may fail to be closed: $\bigcup_{n\ge1}[\tfrac1n,1]=(0,1]$.

The smallest closed set containing $A$, namely $\overline{A}=\bigcap\{F\subseteq X: F\ \text{closed},\ A\subseteq F\}$, is the **closure** of $A$. Two equivalent descriptions are used constantly: first, $x\in\overline{A}$ iff every neighbourhood of $x$ meets $A$ (it suffices to test open neighbourhoods); second, $\overline{A}=A\cup A'$, where $A'$ is the **derived set**: $x\in A'$ means $x$ is a **limit point** of $A$, i.e. every neighbourhood of $x$ meets $A\setminus\{x\}$. A limit point need not belong to $A$ (as $0$ for $(0,1)$), and a point of $A$ need not be a limit point: if some neighbourhood $N$ satisfies $N\cap A=\{x\}$, then $x$ is an **isolated point** of $A$ (every point of $\mathbb{Z}\subset\mathbb{R}$ is one). Hence the clean chain $A$ closed $\iff A'\subseteq A\iff A=\overline{A}$.

Dually, $\operatorname{int}A=\bigcup\{U\in\tau: U\subseteq A\}=X\setminus\overline{X\setminus A}$ is the **interior** of $A$, the largest open set contained in $A$; its members are **interior points** (points having a neighbourhood inside $A$). The **boundary** is $\partial A=\overline{A}\cap\overline{X\setminus A}$, and it cuts the space into three disjoint pieces: $X=\operatorname{int}A\ \sqcup\ \partial A\ \sqcup\ \operatorname{int}(X\setminus A)$. If $\overline{A}=X$ we say $A$ is **dense** in $X$ (equivalently, $A$ meets every nonempty open set), as $\mathbb{Q}$ is in $\mathbb{R}$; if $\operatorname{int}\overline{A}=\varnothing$ we call $A$ **nowhere dense** ($\mathbb{Z}$ in $\mathbb{R}$ is nowhere dense and has no limit points at all, whereas the Cantor set is likewise nowhere dense yet every one of its points is a limit point — so nowhere dense is not the same as having no limit points). A countable union of nowhere dense sets is of **first category**, and a set that is not of first category is of **second category**. The **Baire category theorem** states that complete metric spaces (more generally, locally compact Hausdorff spaces) are of second category — the fact that they cannot be written as a countable union of nowhere dense sets, a fulcrum for many existence theorems.
derivation: 称 $F\subseteq X$ 闭，若 $X\setminus F$ 开。由 De Morgan 律，任意多个闭集之交闭：$X\setminus\bigcap_iF_i=\bigcup_i(X\setminus F_i)$；有限多个闭集之并闭：$X\setminus\bigcup_{k=1}^nF_k=\bigcap_{k=1}^n(X\setminus F_k)$。$\varnothing$ 与 $X$ 既开又闭。但无限并不必闭：$\bigcup_{n\ge1}[1/n,1]=(0,1]$ 在 $\mathbb R$ 中不闭，因为 $0$ 是它的极限点而不属于它。结论：闭集公理与开集公理对偶，仍然是「任意交、有限并」；不要把有限并误推广为任意并。

闭包：令 $\operatorname{cl}A= igcap\{F\subseteq X:F\ 	ext{闭},\ A\subseteq F\}$。该族含 $X$，故不空；任意交闭，故 $\operatorname{cl}A$ 闭；它含 $A$，且任何闭集 $F\supseteq A$ 都出现在交中，故 $\operatorname{cl}A\subseteq F$。因此 $\operatorname{cl}A$ 是含 $A$ 的最小闭集，且 $A$ 闭 $\iff$ $A=\operatorname{cl}A$。点式刻画：$x\in\operatorname{cl}A$ $\iff$ $x$ 的每个邻域都与 $A$ 相交。若 $x
otin\operatorname{cl}A$，则 $X\setminus\operatorname{cl}A$ 是含 $x$ 的开集且与 $A$ 不交，故某个邻域不交；反之若开集 $U
i x$ 与 $A$ 不交，则 $X\setminus U$ 是含 $A$ 的闭集且不含 $x$，故 $x
otin\operatorname{cl}A$。结论：闭包的「全局最小」与「局部每邻域相遇」两种描述等价。

Kuratowski 闭包公理：由定义直接得到 (K1) $A\subseteq\operatorname{cl}A$；(K2) $\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cl}A)=\operatorname{cl}A$；(K3) $\operatorname{cl}(A\cup B)=\operatorname{cl}A\cup\operatorname{cl}B$；(K4) $\operatorname{cl}\varnothing=\varnothing$。K3 证明：$\operatorname{cl}(A\cup B)$ 是含 $A$ 与 $B$ 的闭集，由最小性得 $\operatorname{cl}A\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(A\cup B)$ 与 $\operatorname{cl}B\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(A\cup B)$，故 $\operatorname{cl}A\cup\operatorname{cl}B\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(A\cup B)$；反之 $\operatorname{cl}A\cup\operatorname{cl}B$ 是闭集（有限并）且含 $A\cup B$，由最小性得反向包含。由此也得单调性 $A\subseteq B\Rightarrow\operatorname{cl}A\subseteq\operatorname{cl}B$。但交只有单向：$\operatorname{cl}(A\cap B)\subseteq\operatorname{cl}A\cap\operatorname{cl}B$，且可能严格：$A=\mathbb Q$、$B=\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q$ 时左边为 $\operatorname{cl}\varnothing=\varnothing$，右边为 $\mathbb R$。结论：闭包只对有限并分配，对交不分配。

内部：$\operatorname{int}A=\bigcup\{U\subseteq X:U\ \text{开},\ U\subseteq A\}$。它是开集（任意并）、含于 $A$，且任何开集 $U\subseteq A$ 都含于它，故 $\operatorname{int}A$ 是含于 $A$ 的最大开集；$A$ 开 $\iff$ $A=\operatorname{int}A$。点式：$x\in\operatorname{int}A$ $\iff$ 存在开集 $U$ 使 $x\in U\subseteq A$ $\iff$ $A$ 是 $x$ 的邻域。对偶公式：$\operatorname{int}A=X\setminus\operatorname{cl}(X\setminus A)$。证明：$x\notin\operatorname{int}A$ $\iff$ 每个含 $x$ 的开集都不含于 $A$ $\iff$ 每个含 $x$ 的开集都与 $X\setminus A$ 相交 $\iff$ $x\in\operatorname{cl}(X\setminus A)$。另外 $\operatorname{int}(A\cap B)=\operatorname{int}A\cap\operatorname{int}B$；但 $\operatorname{int}A\cup\operatorname{int}B\subseteq\operatorname{int}(A\cup B)$ 可能严格（$A=(0,1)$、$B=(1,2)$ 时右边为 $(0,2)$）。结论：内部与闭包通过取补对偶；内部是最大开集，闭包是最小闭集。

边界：$\partial A=\operatorname{cl}A\setminus\operatorname{int}A=\operatorname{cl}A\cap\operatorname{cl}(X\setminus A)$，第二个等号用第 4 步的对偶。边界是闭集（两个闭集之交），且 $X=\operatorname{int}A\sqcup\partial A\sqcup\operatorname{int}(X\setminus A)$：三部分分别是「内点」「边界点」「外点」，互不相交且并为 $X$。$\partial A=\partial(X\setminus A)$；$\partial A=\varnothing$ $\iff$ $\operatorname{cl}A=\operatorname{int}A$ $\iff$ $A$ 既开又闭。例：$\mathbb R$ 中 $A=(0,1]$ 的 $\operatorname{cl}A=[0,1]$、$\operatorname{int}A=(0,1)$、$\partial A=\{0,1\}$；而 $A=\mathbb Q$ 的 $\operatorname{cl}A=\mathbb R$、$\operatorname{int}A=\varnothing$、$\partial A=\mathbb R$。结论：边界总是闭集，但可空、可很大，不能凭「边界像端点」的直觉处理一般集合。

稠密：$D$ 在 $X$ 中稠密 $\iff$ $\operatorname{cl}D=X$ $\iff$ $D$ 与每个非空开集相交。证明：若存在非空开 $U$ 与 $D$ 不交，取 $x\in U$，则 $U$ 是 $x$ 的开邻域且不交 $D$，故 $x
otin\operatorname{cl}D$；反之若 $\operatorname{cl}D
e X$，取 $x
otin\operatorname{cl}D$，则 $X\setminus\operatorname{cl}D$ 是非空开集且不交 $D$。$\mathbb Q$ 与 $\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q$ 都在 $\mathbb R$ 中稠密，内部都为空。序列警告：在度量空间（更一般地第一可数空间）中 $x\in\operatorname{cl}A$ $\iff$ 存在 $a_n\in A$ 使 $a_n	o x$；一般拓扑空间不成立。反例：$X$ 不可数，取余可数拓扑 $	au=\{\varnothing\}\cup\{X\setminus C:C\ 	ext{可数}\}$，令 $A=X\setminus\{x\}$。每个非空开集 $X\setminus C$ 不可数，必与 $A$ 相交，故 $x\in\operatorname{cl}A$；但任一序列 $(a_n)\subseteq A$ 的取值集 $S$ 可数，$X\setminus S$ 是含 $x$ 的开集且不含任何 $a_n$，故 $(a_n)$ 不收敛于 $x$。结论：闭包必须用邻域（或网）检验；序列判据在第一可数空间充分，但在一般拓扑空间中未必成立，不能无条件使用。
derivationEn: $F\subseteq X$ is closed if $X\setminus F$ is open. By De Morgan's laws, arbitrary intersections of closed sets are closed: $X\setminus\bigcap_iF_i=\bigcup_i(X\setminus F_i)$; finite unions of closed sets are closed: $X\setminus\bigcup_{k=1}^nF_k=\bigcap_{k=1}^n(X\setminus F_k)$. The sets $\varnothing$ and $X$ are both open and closed. Infinite unions need not be closed: $\bigcup_{n\ge1}[1/n,1]=(0,1]$ is not closed in $\mathbb R$, since $0$ is a limit point not belonging to it. Conclusion: the closed-set axioms are dual to the open-set axioms, again "arbitrary intersections, finite unions"; finite unions must not be generalized to arbitrary ones.

Closure: let $\operatorname{cl}A= igcap\{F\subseteq X:F\ 	ext{closed},\ A\subseteq F\}$. The family is nonempty because it contains $X$; an arbitrary intersection of closed sets is closed, so $\operatorname{cl}A$ is closed; it contains $A$, and every closed $F\supseteq A$ occurs in the intersection, so $\operatorname{cl}A\subseteq F$. Hence $\operatorname{cl}A$ is the smallest closed set containing $A$, and $A$ is closed iff $A=\operatorname{cl}A$. Pointwise description: $x\in\operatorname{cl}A$ iff every neighborhood of $x$ meets $A$. If $x
otin\operatorname{cl}A$, then $X\setminus\operatorname{cl}A$ is an open set containing $x$ and disjoint from $A$, so some neighborhood misses $A$; conversely, if an open $U
i x$ is disjoint from $A$, then $X\setminus U$ is a closed set containing $A$ but not $x$, so $x
otin\operatorname{cl}A$. Conclusion: the global "smallest closed set" and the local "every neighborhood meets $A$" descriptions agree.

Kuratowski closure axioms: directly from the definition, (K1) $A\subseteq\operatorname{cl}A$; (K2) $\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cl}A)=\operatorname{cl}A$; (K3) $\operatorname{cl}(A\cup B)=\operatorname{cl}A\cup\operatorname{cl}B$; (K4) $\operatorname{cl}\varnothing=\varnothing$. For K3: $\operatorname{cl}(A\cup B)$ is a closed set containing $A$ and $B$, so minimality gives $\operatorname{cl}A\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(A\cup B)$ and $\operatorname{cl}B\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(A\cup B)$, hence $\operatorname{cl}A\cup\operatorname{cl}B\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(A\cup B)$; conversely $\operatorname{cl}A\cup\operatorname{cl}B$ is closed (a finite union) and contains $A\cup B$, so minimality gives the reverse inclusion. Monotonicity follows: $A\subseteq B$ implies $\operatorname{cl}A\subseteq\operatorname{cl}B$. Intersections, however, only give one inclusion: $\operatorname{cl}(A\cap B)\subseteq\operatorname{cl}A\cap\operatorname{cl}B$, which may be strict: for $A=\mathbb Q$ and $B=\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q$ the left side is $\operatorname{cl}\varnothing=\varnothing$ while the right side is $\mathbb R$. Conclusion: closure distributes over finite unions but not over intersections.

Interior: $\operatorname{int}A=\bigcup\{U\subseteq X:U\ \text{open},\ U\subseteq A\}$. It is open (an arbitrary union), is contained in $A$, and every open $U\subseteq A$ is contained in it; hence $\operatorname{int}A$ is the largest open set contained in $A$, and $A$ is open iff $A=\operatorname{int}A$. Pointwise: $x\in\operatorname{int}A$ iff there is an open $U$ with $x\in U\subseteq A$, i.e. iff $A$ is a neighborhood of $x$. Duality: $\operatorname{int}A=X\setminus\operatorname{cl}(X\setminus A)$. Indeed, $x\notin\operatorname{int}A$ iff every open set containing $x$ fails to be contained in $A$, iff every open set containing $x$ meets $X\setminus A$, iff $x\in\operatorname{cl}(X\setminus A)$. Also $\operatorname{int}(A\cap B)=\operatorname{int}A\cap\operatorname{int}B$; however $\operatorname{int}A\cup\operatorname{int}B\subseteq\operatorname{int}(A\cup B)$ may be strict (for $A=(0,1)$, $B=(1,2)$ the right side is $(0,2)$). Conclusion: interior and closure are dual under complementation; the interior is the largest open set and the closure the smallest closed set.

Boundary: $\partial A=\operatorname{cl}A\setminus\operatorname{int}A=\operatorname{cl}A\cap\operatorname{cl}(X\setminus A)$, the second equality by Step 4. The boundary is closed (an intersection of two closed sets), and $$X=\operatorname{int}A\;\sqcup\;\partial A\;\sqcup\;\operatorname{int}(X\setminus A):$$ the three parts are the interior points, boundary points, and exterior points; they are pairwise disjoint and cover $X$. Also $\partial A=\partial(X\setminus A)$, and $\partial A=\varnothing$ iff $\operatorname{cl}A=\operatorname{int}A$, iff $A$ is both open and closed. Example: for $A=(0,1]$ in $\mathbb R$, $\operatorname{cl}A=[0,1]$, $\operatorname{int}A=(0,1)$, and $\partial A=\{0,1\}$; for $A=\mathbb Q$, $\operatorname{cl}A=\mathbb R$, $\operatorname{int}A=\varnothing$, and $\partial A=\mathbb R$. Conclusion: the boundary is always closed but may be empty or very large; the intuition that a boundary consists only of endpoints fails for general sets.

Density: $D$ is dense in $X$ iff $\operatorname{cl}D=X$ iff $D$ meets every nonempty open set. Proof: if a nonempty open $U$ misses $D$, take $x\in U$; then $U$ is an open neighborhood of $x$ disjoint from $D$, so $x
otin\operatorname{cl}D$. Conversely, if $\operatorname{cl}D
e X$, take $x
otin\operatorname{cl}D$; then $X\setminus\operatorname{cl}D$ is a nonempty open set disjoint from $D$. Both $\mathbb Q$ and $\mathbb R\setminus\mathbb Q$ are dense in $\mathbb R$, and both have empty interior. Sequential warning: in a metric space (more generally, a first countable space), $x\in\operatorname{cl}A$ iff there is a sequence $a_n\in A$ with $a_n	o x$; this fails in general topological spaces. Counterexample: let $X$ be uncountable with the cocountable topology $	au=\{\varnothing\}\cup\{X\setminus C:C\ 	ext{countable}\}$ and let $A=X\setminus\{x\}$. Every nonempty open set $X\setminus C$ is uncountable and hence meets $A$, so $x\in\operatorname{cl}A$. But for any sequence $(a_n)\subseteq A$ its range $S$ is countable, and $X\setminus S$ is an open set containing $x$ but no term $a_n$; hence $(a_n)$ does not converge to $x$. Conclusion: closures must be tested with neighborhoods (or nets); the sequence criterion is sufficient in first countable spaces but need not hold in general topological spaces and cannot be used unconditionally.

formulas.note: 闭集的定义：补集是开集。这是全部闭集性质的源头。
formulas.noteEn: Definition of a closed set: its complement is open. This is the source of every property of closed sets.

formulas.latex: \overline{A}=\bigcap\{F: F\ \text{闭},\ A\subseteq F\}=A\cup A',\qquad x\in\overline{A}\iff \forall N\in\mathcal{N}(x):\ N\cap A\neq\varnothing
formulas.note: 闭包：含 $A$ 的最小闭集，也等于 $A$ 并上它的聚点；点的判别用「每个邻域都与 $A$ 相交」。
formulas.noteEn: The closure is the smallest closed set containing $A$, equivalently $A$ together with its limit points; membership is tested by every neighbourhood meeting $A$.

formulas.note: 内部：含于 $A$ 的最大开集，与闭包通过取补对偶（开与闭的对称在这里最清楚）。
formulas.noteEn: The interior is the largest open set inside $A$ and is dual to the closure by complementation — the clearest expression of the open/closed symmetry.

formulas.note: 边界定义；空间被剖成三块互不相交的部分（内部、边界、外部）。
formulas.noteEn: Definition of the boundary; the space splits into three disjoint parts (interior, boundary, exterior).

formulas.note: 并的闭包恰等于闭包之并；但交只有单向包含，可能严格（取 $A=\mathbb{Q}$、$B=\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$）。
formulas.noteEn: The closure of a union equals the union of the closures, but for intersections only one inclusion holds and it may be strict (take $A=\mathbb{Q}$, $B=\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$).

properties: 闭包三律：$A\subseteq\overline{A}$、$\overline{\overline{A}}=\overline{A}$、$\overline{A\cup B}=\overline{A}\cup\overline{B}$；且 $A$ 闭 $\iff A=\overline{A}$。但 $\overline{A\cap B}\subseteq\overline{A}\cap\overline{B}$ 可能严格：$A=\mathbb{Q}$、$B=\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ 时 $\overline{A}=\overline{B}=\mathbb{R}$，而 $\overline{A\cap B}=\overline{\varnothing}=\varnothing$

内部与运算：$\operatorname{int}(A\cap B)=\operatorname{int}A\cap\operatorname{int}B$，而 $\operatorname{int}A\cup\operatorname{int}B\subseteq\operatorname{int}(A\cup B)$ 可能严格（$A=(0,1)$、$B=(1,2)$ 时右边为 $(0,2)$）
$A$ 开 $\iff A=\operatorname{int}A$；$\overline{A}$ 是含 $A$ 的最小闭集，$\operatorname{int}A$ 是含于 $A$ 的最大开集；且 $\overline{A}=\operatorname{int}A\sqcup\partial A$

$\partial A=\overline{A}\setminus\operatorname{int}A=\partial(X\setminus A)$ 总是闭集；$\partial A=\varnothing\iff A$ 既开又闭。一般地 $A$ 与 $X\setminus A$ 的开闭组合会出现四种情形（如 $\mathbb{R}$ 中 $(0,1)$、$[0,1]$、$[0,1)$、$\mathbb{R}$）
稠密：$D$ 稠密于 $X\iff\overline{D}=X\iff D$ 与每个非空开集相交；$\mathbb{Q}$ 与 $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ 都在 $\mathbb{R}$ 中稠密且内部都是空的。Baire 纲定理：完备度量空间与局部紧 Hausdorff 空间是第二纲的
propertiesEn: Closure laws: $A\subseteq\overline A$, $\overline{\overline A}=\overline A$, $\overline{A\cup B}=\overline A\cup\overline B$, and $A$ is closed iff $A=\overline A$. However $\overline{A\cap B}\subseteq\overline A\cap\overline B$ may be strict: for $A=\mathbb{Q}$, $B=\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ one has $\overline A=\overline B=\mathbb{R}$ while $\overline{A\cap B}=\varnothing$

Interior and operations: $\operatorname{int}(A\cap B)=\operatorname{int}A\cap\operatorname{int}B$, while $\operatorname{int}A\cup\operatorname{int}B\subseteq\operatorname{int}(A\cup B)$ may be strict ($A=(0,1)$, $B=(1,2)$ give $(0,2)$ on the right)

$A$ is open iff $A=\operatorname{int}A$; $\overline A$ is the smallest closed set containing $A$ and $\operatorname{int}A$ the largest open set inside $A$; moreover $\overline A=\operatorname{int}A\sqcup\partial A$

$\partial A=\overline A\setminus\operatorname{int}A=\partial(X\setminus A)$ is always closed, and $\partial A=\varnothing$ iff $A$ is clopen. In general open/closed status comes in four combinations (e.g. $(0,1)$, $[0,1]$, $[0,1)$, $\mathbb{R}$ in $\mathbb{R}$)

Density: $D$ is dense in $X$ iff $\overline D=X$ iff $D$ meets every nonempty open set; both $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$ are dense in $\mathbb{R}$ with empty interior. The Baire category theorem says complete metric spaces and locally compact Hausdorff spaces are of second category

examples.problem: 求 $A=\mathbb{Q}\cap[0,1]$ 在 $\mathbb{R}$ 中的闭包、内部与边界。
examples.solution:
**闭包**：任取 $x\in[0,1]$ 与 $\varepsilon>0$，由有理数在 $\mathbb{R}$ 中稠密，$(x-\varepsilon,x+\varepsilon)$ 中含有理数 $q$；当 $x\in[0,1]$ 时可取到 $q\in[0,1]$（若取到的 $q$ 落在区间外，因区间与 $[0,1]$ 相交非空，仍可取其中之理数），故 $x\in\overline{A}$。又 $[0,1]$ 是闭集且 $A\subseteq[0,1]$，所以 $\overline{A}\subseteq[0,1]$。于是 $\overline{A}=[0,1]$。
**内部**：任一非空开区间都含无理数，故不含于 $A$；而任何非空开集都含开区间，所以 $A$ 不含非空开集，$\operatorname{int}A=\varnothing$。
**边界**：$\overline{\mathbb{R}\setminus A}=\mathbb{R}$（$\mathbb{R}\setminus A$ 也稠密），故 $\partial A=\overline{A}\cap\overline{\mathbb{R}\setminus A}=[0,1]\cap\mathbb{R}=[0,1]$。
结论：$A$ 稠密于 $[0,1]$、内部为空、边界是整个 $[0,1]$，可见「稠密」与「内部大」毫无关系。

examples.problem: 举例说明 $\overline{A\cap B}\subsetneq\overline{A}\cap\overline{B}$，即在 $\mathbb{R}$ 中找出两个集合使包含号严格取到。
examples.solution:
取 $A=\mathbb{Q}$，$B=\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$。
一方面 $\overline{A}=\mathbb{R}$（有理数稠密），$\overline{B}=\mathbb{R}$（无理数也稠密），故 $\overline{A}\cap\overline{B}=\mathbb{R}$。
另一方面 $A\cap B=\varnothing$，其闭包是 $\varnothing$。
于是 $\varnothing=\overline{A\cap B}\subsetneq\mathbb{R}=\overline{A}\cap\overline{B}$，包含号严格。这说明「取闭包」只对**并**保持等式，对**交**只能得到单向包含。
（对偶地，取内部时 $\operatorname{int}(A\cup B)$ 可能严格大于 $\operatorname{int}A\cup\operatorname{int}B$：$A=(0,1)$、$B=(1,2)$ 时左边是 $(0,2)$，右边是 $(0,1)\cup(1,2)$。）

continuity-homeomorphism.definition:
$f:X\to Y$ 称为**连续**，若每个开集的原像是开集：对任意 $U\subseteq Y$ 开，$f^{-1}(U)=\{x\in X: f(x)\in U\}$ 都开。**关键词是「原像」**，连续性与「像是不是开集」毫无关系。等价刻画有四条常用路线：（i）任意闭集的原像是闭集；（ii）对任意 $A\subseteq X$ 有 $f(\overline{A})\subseteq\overline{f(A)}$；（iii）对任意 $B\subseteq Y$ 有 $\overline{f^{-1}(B)}\subseteq f^{-1}(\overline{B})$；（iv）逐点形式——$f$ 在 $x$ 处连续指 $f(x)$ 的每个邻域 $V$ 都含某个 $x$ 的邻域 $U$ 的像：$f(U)\subseteq V$。

第（ii）条最容易记错：它**只能**是 $f(\overline{A})\subseteq\overline{f(A)}$，一般不是等式。$f(x)=\dfrac{x}{1+|x|}$（连续，把 $\mathbb{R}$ 压进 $(-1,1)$）与 $A=(0,+\infty)$ 就给出严格包含：$f(\overline{A})=[0,1)$，而 $\overline{f(A)}=[0,1]$。直觉上，闭包会「补上极限点」，而连续映射可能把极限点送到像集之外的极限点上。

连续与「把开集映成开集」是两件不同的事，两者互不推出：常值映射 $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$，$f(x)=0$ 连续，却把开集 $(0,1)$ 映成单点集 $\{0\}$，不是开集；反过来令 $X=\{a,b\}$ 带平凡拓扑、$Y=\{a,b\}$ 带离散拓扑，$f(x)=x$，则 $X$ 的开集只有 $\varnothing,X$，像也开，故 $f$ 是开映射，但 $f^{-1}(\{a\})=\{a\}$ 在 $X$ 中不 open，故 $f$ 不连续。因此「开映射」是一条独立的要求，不可与连续混为一谈。

若 $f:X\to Y$ 是双射，且 $f$ 连续、$f^{-1}$ 也连续，就称 $f$ 是**同胚**（homeomorphism），记 $X\cong Y$。等价地说：$f$ 连续双射且是开映射（或闭映射）。**仅连续双射不够**：经典例子是 $f(t)=(\cos2\pi t,\sin2\pi t)$，$f:[0,1)\to S^1$ 是连续双射，但 $f^{-1}$ 在 $(1,0)$ 处不连续，故不同胚。不过加一个条件就够用了：**连续双射 + 定义域紧 + 目标空间 Hausdorff $\Rightarrow$ 同胚**。

同胚是集合之间的**等价关系**（自反、对称、传递），因此拓扑学只区分「同胚类」。被同胚保持的性质叫**拓扑性质**：紧致性、连通性、Hausdorff 性、可分性、第二可数性都是；有界性与完备性不是（$\mathbb{R}\cong(0,1)$，后者有界且不完备）。若 $f:X\to Y$ 连续单射，且从 $X$ 到子空间 $f(X)$ 的对应是同胚，就称 $f$ 是**嵌入**（拓扑嵌入）——嵌入是「把 $X$ 原样放进 $Y$ 里」。
continuity-homeomorphism.definitionEn:
A map $f:X\to Y$ is **continuous** if the preimage of every open set is open: for every open $U\subseteq Y$, the set $f^{-1}(U)=\{x\in X: f(x)\in U\}$ is open in $X$. **The key word is preimage**; continuity says nothing about images being open. Four equivalent formulations are in constant use: (i) preimages of closed sets are closed; (ii) $f(\overline{A})\subseteq\overline{f(A)}$ for every $A\subseteq X$; (iii) $\overline{f^{-1}(B)}\subseteq f^{-1}(\overline{B})$ for every $B\subseteq Y$; (iv) pointwise — $f$ is continuous at $x$ if every neighbourhood $V$ of $f(x)$ contains the image of some neighbourhood $U$ of $x$: $f(U)\subseteq V$.

Formulation (ii) is the one most often misquoted: it is **only** $f(\overline{A})\subseteq\overline{f(A)}$, never equality in general. With $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{1+|x|}$ (continuous, squeezing $\mathbb{R}$ into $(-1,1)$) and $A=(0,+\infty)$ the inclusion is strict: $f(\overline{A})=[0,1)$ while $\overline{f(A)}=[0,1]$. Intuitively, taking a closure adjoins limit points, and a continuous map may send a limit point to a limit point lying outside the image.

Continuity and mapping open sets to open sets are different demands, and neither implies the other: the constant map $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, $f(x)=0$, is continuous yet sends the open interval $(0,1)$ to the singleton $\{0\}$, not open; conversely let $X=\{a,b\}$ carry the trivial topology and $Y=\{a,b\}$ the discrete topology, with $f(x)=x$. The only open sets of $X$ are $\varnothing$ and $X$, whose images are open, so $f$ is an open map, yet $f^{-1}(\{a\})=\{a\}$ is not open in $X$, so $f$ is not continuous. Being an open map is thus an independent requirement.

If $f:X\to Y$ is a bijection with $f$ and $f^{-1}$ both continuous, $f$ is a **homeomorphism**, written $X\cong Y$. Equivalently: $f$ is a continuous bijection which is an open map (or a closed map). **A continuous bijection alone is not enough**: the classic example is $f(t)=(\cos2\pi t,\sin2\pi t)$, a continuous bijection $[0,1)\to S^1$ whose inverse is discontinuous at $(1,0)$, so it is not a homeomorphism. One extra hypothesis suffices: **continuous bijection + compact domain + Hausdorff target $\Rightarrow$ homeomorphism**.

Homeomorphism is an **equivalence relation** (reflexive, symmetric, transitive), so topology classifies spaces only up to homeomorphism. Properties preserved by it are called **topological**: compactness, connectedness, the Hausdorff property, separability, second countability. Boundedness and completeness are not ($\mathbb{R}\cong(0,1)$, the latter bounded and incomplete). If $f:X\to Y$ is a continuous injection which is a homeomorphism onto the subspace $f(X)$, then $f$ is an **embedding** — the precise sense in which $X$ sits inside $Y$ unchanged.
derivation: 定义：$f:X\to Y$ 连续，若对每个开集 $U\subseteq Y$，$f^{-1}(U)\subseteq X$ 开。原像与并、交、补交换：$$\begin{aligned}f^{-1}\Bigl(\bigcup_\alpha U_\alpha\Bigr)&=\bigcup_\alpha f^{-1}(U_\alpha),\\ f^{-1}\Bigl(\bigcap_\alpha U_\alpha\Bigr)&=\bigcap_\alpha f^{-1}(U_\alpha),\\ f^{-1}(Y\setminus B)&=X\setminus f^{-1}(B).\end{aligned}$$ 因此连续 $\iff$ 每个闭集的原像闭。像没有这种性质：常值映射 $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$、$f(x)=0$ 连续，却把开集 $(0,1)$ 映成单点 $\{0\}$，不是开集。反之，开映射也不必连续：$X=\{a,b\}$ 取平凡拓扑、$Y=\{a,b\}$ 取离散拓扑，恒等映射把开集映成开集，但 $\{a\}$ 的原像 $\{a\}$ 在 $X$ 中不开。结论：连续性的条件是「开集的原像开」，不是「开集的像开」；连续与开映射是两个互不包含的概念。

i x$ 使 $f(U_x)\subseteq V$，则 $U_x\subseteq f^{-1}(V)$，故 $f^{-1}(V)= igcup_{x\in f^{-1}(V)}U_x$ 开。若 $\mathcal B$ 是 $Y$ 的基，则 $f$ 连续 $\iff$ 每个 $B\in\mathcal B$ 的原像开：任一开 $V= igcup_\alpha B_\alpha$ 的原像是 $ igcup_\alpha f^{-1}(B_\alpha)$。子基同理（先取有限交再取并）。结论：连续性可在每点局部验证，也可只在目标空间的一组生成元上验证；度量空间中取开球即得 $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ 定义。

同胚：若 $f:X\to Y$ 是双射且 $f$ 与 $f^{-1}$ 都连续，称 $f$ 为同胚，记 $X\cong Y$。等价刻画：双射 $f$ 是同胚 $\iff$ $f$ 连续且为开映射。证明：若 $f^{-1}$ 连续，则对开 $U\subseteq X$，$f(U)=(f^{-1})^{-1}(U)$ 开，故 $f$ 开；反之若 $f$ 连续、开且双射，则对开 $U\subseteq X$，$(f^{-1})^{-1}(U)=f(U)$ 开，故 $f^{-1}$ 连续。同胚是等价关系：恒等、逆、复合均保持。被同胚保持的性质叫拓扑性质，如紧致性、连通性、Hausdorff 性、可分性、第二可数性；有界性与完备性不是：$\mathbb R\cong(0,1)$，后者有界且不完备。结论：同胚是拓扑学中「相同」的正确含义，但定义中的逆连续性不能省略。

连续双射不必同胚：$f:[0,1)\to S^1$，$f(t)=(\cos2\pi t,\sin2\pi t)$。$f$ 连续（两个分量连续），且是双射：圆周上每点有唯一角 $\theta\in[0,2\pi)$，对应 $t=\theta/(2\pi)\in[0,1)$。若 $f$ 是同胚，则 $f^{-1}:S^1\to[0,1)$ 连续；$S^1$ 是 $\mathbb R^2$ 中的有界闭集，故紧，连续像是紧的，于是 $[0,1)=f^{-1}(S^1)$ 紧。但 $[0,1)$ 不紧：开覆盖 $\{[0,1-1/n):n\ge2\}$ 没有有限子覆盖。矛盾。也可直接看 $A=[1/2,1)$ 在 $[0,1)$ 中开，而 $f(A)$ 是不含 $(1,0)$ 的下半圆弧，在 $(-1,0)$ 处不是 $S^1$ 中的开集，故 $f$ 不是开映射。结论：连续双射只保证「一一对应且连续」，不保证逆连续；同胚确实更强。

紧–Hausdorff 升级：设 $f:X\to Y$ 连续双射，$X$ 紧，$Y$ Hausdorff，则 $f$ 是同胚。证明：只需证 $f$ 是闭映射。设 $F\subseteq X$ 闭，紧空间的闭子集 $F$ 紧；连续像 $f(F)$ 紧；Hausdorff 空间的紧子集闭，故 $f(F)$ 闭。于是双射 $f$ 把闭集映成闭集，等价地把开集映成开集：$f(U)=Y\setminus f(X\setminus U)$；由第 4 步 $f^{-1}$ 连续。两个条件都必要：$[0,1)\to S^1$ 说明 $X$ 不紧时结论失败；两点离散空间到两点平凡拓扑空间的恒等映射是连续双射，但目标不 Hausdorff，逆不连续。推论：紧空间到 Hausdorff 空间的连续单射是到像上的同胚，即嵌入。结论：紧性加 Hausdorff 性把连续双射免费升级为同胚，这是最常用的判据。
derivationEn: Definition: $f:X\to Y$ is continuous if $f^{-1}(U)\subseteq X$ is open for every open $U\subseteq Y$. Preimages commute with unions, intersections and complements: $$\begin{aligned}f^{-1}\Bigl(\bigcup_\alpha U_\alpha\Bigr)&=\bigcup_\alpha f^{-1}(U_\alpha),\\ f^{-1}\Bigl(\bigcap_\alpha U_\alpha\Bigr)&=\bigcap_\alpha f^{-1}(U_\alpha),\\ f^{-1}(Y\setminus B)&=X\setminus f^{-1}(B).\end{aligned}$$ Hence $f$ is continuous iff preimages of closed sets are closed. Images have no such property: the constant map $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, $f(x)=0$, is continuous but sends the open set $(0,1)$ to the singleton $\{0\}$, which is not open. Conversely, an open map need not be continuous: let $X=\{a,b\}$ carry the trivial topology and $Y=\{a,b\}$ the discrete topology; the identity sends open sets to open sets, but the preimage of $\{a\}$ is $\{a\}$, which is not open in $X$. Conclusion: continuity is a condition on preimages of open sets, not on images; continuity and being an open map are two notions, neither implying the other.

Closure characterization: $f$ is continuous iff $f(\operatorname{cl}A)\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(f(A))$ for every $A\subseteq X$. Proof: assume $f$ continuous and let $x\in\operatorname{cl}A$. For any neighborhood $V$ of $f(x)$, choose an open $V'
i f(x)$ with $V'\subseteq V$ and put $U=f^{-1}(V')$; then $U$ is open, contains $x$, and $f(U)\subseteq V$; since $U\cap A
e\varnothing$, also $V\cap f(A)
e\varnothing$, so $f(x)\in\operatorname{cl}(f(A))$. Conversely, assume the inclusion and let $F\subseteq Y$ be closed; put $A=f^{-1}(F)$. Then $f(\operatorname{cl}A)\subseteq\operatorname{cl}(f(A))\subseteq\operatorname{cl}F=F$, so $\operatorname{cl}A\subseteq f^{-1}(F)=A$ and $A$ is closed. An equivalent form is $\operatorname{cl}(f^{-1}(B))\subseteq f^{-1}(\operatorname{cl}B)$. The inclusion is generally strict: for $f(x)=x/(1+|x|)$ and $A=(0,+\infty)$, $f(\operatorname{cl}A)=[0,1)$ while $\operatorname{cl}(f(A))=[0,1]$. Conclusion: a continuous map sends closures into the closure of the image, but does not preserve equality.

Pointwise and generating families: $f$ is continuous at $x$ if for every neighborhood $V$ of $f(x)$ there is a neighborhood $U$ of $x$ with $f(U)\subseteq V$; equivalently, for every open $V
i f(x)$ there is an open $U
i x$ with $f(U)\subseteq V$. Then $f$ is continuous iff it is continuous at every point: for necessity, given a neighborhood $V$ of $f(x)$, take an open $V'\subseteq V$ with $f(x)\in V'$ and set $U=f^{-1}(V')$, so $U$ is a neighborhood of $x$ and $f(U)\subseteq V$; for sufficiency, given open $V\subseteq Y$ and $x\in f^{-1}(V)$, choose an open $U_x
i x$ with $f(U_x)\subseteq V$; then $U_x\subseteq f^{-1}(V)$, so $f^{-1}(V)= igcup_{x\in f^{-1}(V)}U_x$ is open. If $\mathcal B$ is a basis for $Y$, then $f$ is continuous iff $f^{-1}(B)$ is open for every $B\in\mathcal B$: any open $V= igcup_\alpha B_\alpha$ has $f^{-1}(V)= igcup_\alpha f^{-1}(B_\alpha)$. The same holds for a subbasis (take finite intersections first, then unions). Conclusion: continuity can be checked locally at each point and on a generating family of the target; in metric spaces, taking open balls gives the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ definition.

Homeomorphism: a bijection $f:X\to Y$ is a homeomorphism, written $X\cong Y$, if both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are continuous. Equivalent description: a bijection $f$ is a homeomorphism iff $f$ is continuous and open. Proof: if $f^{-1}$ is continuous, then for open $U\subseteq X$ the set $f(U)=(f^{-1})^{-1}(U)$ is open, so $f$ is open; conversely, if $f$ is continuous, open and bijective, then for open $U\subseteq X$, $(f^{-1})^{-1}(U)=f(U)$ is open, so $f^{-1}$ is continuous. Homeomorphism is an equivalence relation: identity, inverse and composites preserve it. Properties preserved by homeomorphisms are called topological: compactness, connectedness, the Hausdorff property, separability, second countability; boundedness and completeness are not: $\mathbb R\cong(0,1)$, and the latter is bounded and incomplete. Conclusion: homeomorphism is the correct notion of sameness in topology, but the continuity of the inverse in the definition cannot be omitted.

A continuous bijection need not be a homeomorphism: $f:[0,1)\to S^1$, $f(t)=(\cos2\pi t,\sin2\pi t)$. It is continuous (both components are continuous) and bijective: every point of the circle has a unique angle $\theta\in[0,2\pi)$, corresponding to $t=\theta/(2\pi)\in[0,1)$. If $f$ were a homeomorphism, then $f^{-1}:S^1\to[0,1)$ would be continuous; $S^1$ is a bounded closed subset of $\mathbb R^2$, hence compact, and a continuous image of a compact space is compact, so $[0,1)=f^{-1}(S^1)$ would be compact. But $[0,1)$ is not compact: the open cover $\{[0,1-1/n):n\ge2\}$ has no finite subcover. Alternatively, $A=[1/2,1)$ is open in $[0,1)$, while $f(A)$ is the lower semicircle without $(1,0)$, which is not open in $S^1$ at $(-1,0)$; so $f$ is not an open map. Conclusion: a continuous bijection only gives a one-to-one continuous correspondence, not continuity of the inverse; being a homeomorphism is genuinely stronger.

Compact–Hausdorff upgrade: if $f:X\to Y$ is a continuous bijection, $X$ is compact and $Y$ is Hausdorff, then $f$ is a homeomorphism. Proof: it suffices to show that $f$ is closed. Let $F\subseteq X$ be closed; a closed subset $F$ of a compact space is compact; its continuous image $f(F)$ is compact; a compact subset of a Hausdorff space is closed, so $f(F)$ is closed. Thus the bijection $f$ sends closed sets to closed sets, equivalently sends open sets to open sets: $f(U)=Y\setminus f(X\setminus U)$; by Step 4, $f^{-1}$ is continuous. Both hypotheses are needed: $[0,1)\to S^1$ shows that the conclusion fails when $X$ is not compact; the identity from a two-point discrete space to a two-point indiscrete space is a continuous bijection whose inverse is discontinuous, so the target must be Hausdorff. Corollary: a continuous injection from a compact space into a Hausdorff space is an embedding, i.e. a homeomorphism onto its image. Conclusion: compactness plus Hausdorffness upgrades a continuous bijection to a homeomorphism for free, which is the most useful criterion.
